chapter_theme: Lack of learning (கல்லாமை), where learning means knowing Siva: the unlearned take the passing for the lasting, cannot see the Lord in their hearts and suffer their deeds, while those who know the true reckoning have truly learned; book learning without Siva-knowledge or love is itself a kind of unlearning.
structure_note: The chapter keeps turning the word கல்லாதார்: the unlearned who see by grace (310) and the poet's own unlearning (313) stand beside the unlearned who cannot see the Lord (311, 312, 314, 317), and the learned who lack Siva-knowledge (315, 318, 319). 316 defines the truly learned as those who know the கணக்கு.

310.reading: Even the unlearned, if skilled in the vision that knows the meaning, are valued by the eye of grace; the unlearned hold to the truth, and even the learned cannot see the joy of the unlearned.
310.nuance: The verse is hard to construe. பற்றா நிற்பர் can mean 'stand holding' or 'stand not holding' the truth, and the last line can mean that the learned cannot see the joy of the unlearned or that the learned, like the unlearned, do not see joy. Against the rest of the chapter it seems to allow a graced unlearning that sees what learning misses.

311.reading: The able always live joined to the one way, while the others say knowledge is many; our God is in every place, but the unlearned do not know his being mingled in all.
311.nuance: வல்லார், the able, stands for the truly learned. அறிவு பல, 'knowledge is many', is taken as the many doctrines of the sects. கலப்பு may be his pervasion of all or the soul's union with him.

312.reading: You who feel in your heart that the state which does not stay is lasting, and that this perishing hut is permanent: though he is the Lord of all lives, he cannot be seen in the hearts of the unlearned.
312.nuance: குரம்பை, a hut or nest, is the body. The verse ties lack of learning to one specific error, taking the impermanent for the lasting.

313.reading: I could not; I fell into the delusion that makes the suffering of deeds; I did not learn, being one who did not know Hara's way; yet with the Giver in my mind, I, unlearned, can go beyond and dance.
313.nuance: A first-person confession whose turn is from கல்லேன் (I did not learn) to வல்லேன் (I am able). I take 'the Giver' (வழங்கும் பொருள்) as the Lord whose grace makes up what learning did not; ஆடவல்லேன் may echo the Lord's name ஆடவல்லான், the dancer. The first word கில்லேன் and the second line's syntax are uncertain.

314.reading: Thinking that life does not stay and is not lasting, the able have entered virtue and tapas; the unlearned men, the base of the world, live out the suffering of evil deeds.
314.nuance: The able here act on impermanence, by virtue and austerity; the unlearned simply undergo it. கயவர், the base, is the word of the Kural's chapter on baseness.

315.reading: The shining fruit that ripened within the sky was mingled within the eye and stayed there; yet those within the earth reckoned and reckoned, thought and wrote, and wore themselves out.
315.nuance: The plain point is that what scholars seek in books is already near. Traditionally the sky is the inner space at the crown, the eye the point between the brows, and the fruit Siva's light seen in yoga; the verse does not say so, and both readings stand.

316.reading: It cannot be seen except by those who know the reckoning, and the vision is not won except by them; knowing the reckoning, they see the truth and stand to reach it; those who know the reckoning are the ones who have learned.
316.nuance: கணக்கு, the word repeated in every line, means account, measure or method; it is traditionally taken as the right order of knowing (of the tattvas, or of the path), not arithmetic. அண்ட நிற்கும் is unclear: perhaps 'stand near', perhaps 'stand in the cosmos'.

317.reading: One should not even look upon unlearned fools, nor is it one's duty to hear their words; beside unlearned fools the merely unlearned are good; unlearned fools do not know the meaning.
317.nuance: The third line separates the unlearned fool (கல்லாத மூடர்) from the plainly unlearned, who are better. It can also be read 'to unlearned fools, the unlearned seem good', that is, fools prize their own kind.

318.reading: Wretches who have learned yet lack Siva-knowledge do not leave their kin or rid themselves of fault; they are fools, and the witless do not see the many directions; those who stand in love after learning are the ones who know the reckoning.
318.nuance: The chapter's sharpest claim: learning without சிவஞானம் leaves one among the fools. சுற்றமும் வீடார் may also pun on வீடு, release. The last line joins love to learning and recalls 316's கணக்கறிந்தார்.

319.reading: He is the First Lord, the supreme flame even to the immortals, the great god whom the devotees of light follow; people say 'we can recite and know him', but they do not know the course of the light that stands within and moves them.
319.nuance: சோதி comes three times: the supreme light, the light followed by devotees, and the light within that directs (நடத்தும்) the person. Claimed knowledge by recitation misses the last.

links.note: Both deny learning its fruit without the Lord: the Kural asks what learning gains if one does not worship the feet of the one of pure knowledge, Tirumular calls the learned without Siva-knowledge wretches and fools.

The Kural makes learning the eyes and gives the unlearned two sores; 310, if read as it seems, gives sight to the unlearned who have the grace-eye and denies the learned their joy. The contrast depends on reading கல்லாதவர் as the book-unlearned.
The Kural finds the unlearned very good if they keep silent before the learned; Tirumular will not even look at or listen to unlearned fools, though he too grants that the merely unlearned are good.
315 mocks those who reckoned and wrote till they wore out; 316 keeps reckoning (கணக்கு) but makes the true one the only way to see. Reckoning is not rejected, only the wrong kind.

source_issues: 310 and 313 are hard to construe; 313 line 1 (கில்லேன்) may be corrupt.
